source_refs.note: Topic 3.3.2 (PDF 73-74, printed 70-71). The book counts n! routes; the (n - 1)!/2 refinement is general knowledge and is flagged. Short question 3 is answered.

items: Tractable: solvable in polynomial time, so the time grows at a manageable rate with input size; such problems are 'efficiently solvable'. Example: sorting with Merge Sort or Quick Sort, O(n log n).

Intractable: needs super-polynomial time, often exponential, so it is impractical for large inputs. Example: the Travelling Salesman Problem (TSP), finding the shortest route that visits a set of cities and returns to the start; it is NP-hard.

blocks.text: The number of possible routes grows factorially: n! means multiplying all whole numbers from n down to 1. For 2 cities 2! = 2, for 3 cities 3! = 6, for 4 cities 4! = 24. Strictly, with a fixed starting city and ignoring direction there are (n - 1)!/2 different round trips, but this count also grows factorially.

blocks.prompt: Compare tractable and intractable problems (short question 3).
blocks.explanation: Both are solvable, but tractable problems have polynomial-time algorithms whose running time stays manageable as input grows (sorting), while intractable problems need super-polynomial time, so exact solutions become infeasible for large inputs (TSP with many cities).

items: Tractable: polynomial time (merge sort O(n log n)). Intractable: super-polynomial (TSP, routes grow like n!).
